content.content: # Job — Extend the task tracker The directory holds a working program in Miri: a task tracker that reads commands from a file and reports what it did. Extend it. The program's source is at `main.mi`. Build and run it with the `miri` compiler: `miri check`, `miri build`, `miri run` and `miri test`. ## What it already does The first command-line argument is the path of a text file holding one command per line. Blank lines are ignored. | Command | What it does | |---|---| | `add ` | Records a task, open, and writes `added <id>`. Ids start at 1 and count up. The title is the rest of the line and may hold spaces. | | `done <id>` | Marks that task finished and writes `done <id>`; writes `no such task <id>` when no task has that id. | | `list` | Writes every open task as `<id> <title>`, in the order the tasks were added. | ## What to add 1. `prio <id> <p>` sets a task's priority, where `p` is a digit from 0 to 9, and writes `prio <id> <p>`. A task nobody set a priority on has priority 5. An id no task has writes `no such task <id>`; a `p` outside 0 to 9 writes `bad priority <p>` and changes nothing. 2. `list` now orders the open tasks by priority, ascending, and breaks ties by id, ascending. Its line format does not change. 3. `list all` writes **every** task, finished ones included, under the same order, as `<mark> <id> <title>` — where the mark is `-` for an open task and `x` for a finished one. 4. A line whose first word is none of these commands writes `? <word>`, naming that first word. Today the program ignores such a line. Everything the program already does keeps working exactly as it does now. ## Done The job is finished when the program builds, the four additions behave as written, and the original three commands are unchanged. There are no tests in the directory; the contract above is the specification. total 16 drwxr-xr-x 4 vshynkarenko staff 128 11 Okt. 15:48 . drwxr-xr-x 5 vshynkarenko staff 160 11 Okt. 15:48 .. -rw-r--r-- 1 vshynkarenko staff 1881 11 Okt. 15:48 BRIEF.md -rw-r--r-- 1 vshynkarenko staff 1737 13 Sep. 17:41 main.mi

/// A small task tracker.

use system.fs
use system.os
use system.collections.list

public class Task
    public var id int
    public var title String
    public var done bool

    public fn init(id int, title String)
        self.id = id
        self.title = title
        self.done = false

fn find(tasks [Task], id int) Task?
    for task in tasks
        if task.id == id
            return Some(task)
    return None

fn read_commands(path String) [String]
    let fs = Fs()
    let contents = match fs.read_file(path)
        Result.Ok(text): text
        Result.Err(_error): ""
    return contents.trim_end().split("\n")

fn first_word(line String) String
    return line.split(" ").element_at(0)

fn rest_of(line String) String
    let head = first_word(line)
    if line.length() == head.length()
        return ""
    return line.substring(head.length() + 1, line.length())

fn main()
    let args = Args()
    var tasks = List<Task>()
    var next_id = 1

    for line in read_commands(args.element_at(0))
        if line == ""
            continue
        let command = first_word(line)
        let rest = rest_of(line)

        if command == "add"
            tasks.push(Task(next_id, rest))
            println(f"added {next_id}")
            next_id = next_id + 1
        else if command == "done"
            let id = rest.to_int() ?? 0
            match find(tasks, id)
                Some(found):
                    var task = found
                    task.done = true
                    println(f"done {id}")
                None: println(f"no such task {id}")
        else if command == "list"
            for task in tasks
                if not task.done
                    println(f"{task.id} {task.title}")

s=open('main.mi').read()
s=s.replace("""    public var done bool

""","""    public var done bool
    public var priority int

""").replace("""        self.done = false
""","""        self.done = false
        self.priority = 5
""")
s=s.replace("""fn main()""","""fn is_priority(text String) bool
    if text.length() != 1
        return false
    let value = text.to_int() ?? -1
    return value >= 0 and value <= 9

fn list_tasks(tasks [Task], all bool)
    for p in 0..10
        for task in tasks
            if task.priority != p
                continue
            if all
                let mark = if task.done then "x" else "-"
                println(f"{mark} {task.id} {task.title}")
            else if not task.done
                println(f"{task.id} {task.title}")

fn main()""")
i=s.index('        else if command == "list"')
s=s[:i]+'''        else if command == "prio"
            let parts = rest.split(" ")
            let id = parts.element_at(0).to_int() ?? 0
            var arg = ""
            if parts.length() > 1
                arg = parts.element_at(1)
            match find(tasks, id)
                Some(found):
                    if is_priority(arg)
                        var task = found
                        task.priority = arg.to_int() ?? 5
                        println(f"prio {id} {arg}")
                    else
                        println(f"bad priority {arg}")
                None: println(f"no such task {id}")
        else if command == "list"
            list_tasks(tasks, rest == "all")
        else
            println(f"? {command}")
'''

I extended `main.mi` with all four additions. It type-checks, and a run over a sample command file gave the expected output. - **`prio

`**: tasks default to priority 5. It writes `prio

`, `no such task ` or `bad priority

` as specified. - **`list`**: open tasks come out by priority ascending, then id ascending, in the same line format as before. - **`list all`**: every task is written as ` ` in the same order, with `-` for open and `x` for finished. - **Unknown commands**: a line with an unrecognised first word writes `? <word>`. If `prio` gets both an unknown id and a bad priority, it reports `no such task`. The brief doesn't say which should win. The sample run exercised each of those paths, but only that one file; I didn't separately re-check the original `add`, `done` and `list` behaviour. I changed nothing in their code beyond routing `list` through the new function.
